final_answer:
BOTTOM LINE. Yes, he has recourse, and the sequence matters: first fix the removal order, then fix the USCIS denials.

1. What to file with the immigration court (as of April 1, 2026). File a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order with the immigration court that entered it, under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). The ground is lack of notice: the order may be rescinded 'upon a motion to reopen filed at any time' if the alien did not receive notice under INA 239(a)(1) or (2). The NTA was mailed to an address he never supplied. In absentia removal requires proof that written notice was given (INA 240(b)(5)(A)), and the INA 240(b)(5)(B) exception (no notice needed where the alien failed to provide an address) should not apply because he was never served the NTA that carries the address-reporting duty. There is no deadline for a lack-of-notice motion, so the 180-day exceptional-circumstances window (which ran about January 28, 2026) is irrelevant. Filing the motion automatically stays removal while it is pending before the IJ (INA 240(b)(5)(C); 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)); the stay does not extend to a BIA appeal if it is denied. Practically: confirm the court and case status (EOIR automated case information), enter an appearance, and file the motion with the court's practice-manual requirements (cover page, proof of service on DHS/ICE, a sworn declaration from the husband explaining that he never received the NTA or hearing notice and had never given that address, evidence of his actual address and of the USCIS filings showing his correct address, the same facts for the RFE, and evidence of the wrong-address mailing). Include the relief application he would pursue if reopened (the I-485 as adjustment relief; the court's rules may require attaching it, or an I-130 receipt/approval). Add a request to stay removal in the alternative. The key legal weakness to anticipate is DHS arguing that a notice of hearing was sent to a valid address; here the NTA and the hearing notices appear to have followed the wrong address, so the record should be checked for the actual address of record with EOIR. Supreme Court cases on notice (Pereira v. Sessions; Niz-Chavez v. Garland; Campos-Chaves v. Garland (2024), which allows a later separate hearing notice to cure for in absentia purposes but still requires that notice actually be sent to the proper address) frame the argument; I did not verify their text in this run.

2. Fees. Based on secondary sources (not primary text, which I could not retrieve): a motion to reopen an in absentia order under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (lack of notice) carries no EOIR filing fee, by statute/regulation (cited as 8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)(iii)), and the 2025 H.R.1 (OBBBA) surcharge does not apply to such a motion. Other IJ motions to reopen cost far more (reported total about $1,045 after the H.R.1 add-on), so the motion should be framed and labelled as a lack-of-notice motion under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii). Reported EOIR fee increases effective October 1, 2026 postdate April 1, 2026. The separate in absentia fee (about $5,130, assessed after ICE apprehension) is avoided if the order is rescinded for lack of notice. Verify current amounts on the EOIR fee schedule before filing.

3. Contesting the USCIS denials. (a) I-485: a denial of an I-485 is not appealable to the AAO; if the removal case is reopened, the husband can renew the I-485 before the IJ (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)), which is the realistic path once he is in proceedings. This requires an approved or approvable I-130 (immediate relative of a US citizen, INA 201(b)(2)(A)(i), 245(a); the 245(c) bars generally do not apply to immediate relatives). Note that while the in absentia order stands, INA 240(b)(7) bars adjustment for ten years after a non-excused failure to appear, so rescission is essential. (b) I-130: denial for abandonment (no RFE response) cannot be appealed, but a motion to reopen may be filed under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15) and 103.5(a)(2), with evidence that the RFE was sent to an address other than the one on the filing (Form I-290B). The 30-day deadline (33 if mailed) in 103.5(a)(1) is long past (December 2023), but USCIS may excuse delay where it was reasonable and beyond the filer's control; the couple's belief that the case was pending, caused by the RFE and denial notices going to the wrong address, supports that. If the wrong-address mailing is confirmed by the case record, also ask USCIS to reopen sua sponte (103.5(a)(5)). Because discretionary excusal is uncertain, the safe parallel step is to file a new I-130 (and, in proceedings, the court I-485), since a marriage-based I-130 is not time-barred. If the IJ reopens, DHS or the IJ may also continue/administratively close the case pending the I-130. (c) Risks to flag: the marriage 19 days after a B-2 entry within the 90-day window invites a preconceived-intent/misrepresentation inquiry (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i)), and the I-130 needs a bona fide marriage showing. The AR-11 duty to keep addresses current should also be handled immediately.

CAVEATS. I could not open primary-source text for the statute, 8 CFR 1003.23/1003.24, or the EOIR fee rule because fetches were blocked, so the statutory and fee propositions rest on search-result summaries and my background knowledge and should be confirmed before filing.

What must be filed with immigration court and where; automatic stay
EOIR fees as of April 1, 2026 (H.R.1 changes; lack-of-notice exemption)
Recourse for I-130 abandonment denial after RFE mailed to wrong address (8 CFR 103.2(b)(15), 103.5)

Notice cases (Pereira, Niz-Chavez, Campos-Chaves, Laparra) and counterargument that notice of hearing went to valid address

claims.text: The husband may file a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order for lack of notice with the immigration court at any time; no deadline.
Filing triggers an automatic stay of removal pending IJ decision.
No EOIR fee applies to a 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) lack-of-notice motion (H.R.1 surcharge inapplicable); per secondary summaries, to be confirmed.
I-130 abandonment denial can be challenged by USCIS motion to reopen showing RFE went to wrong address; delay may be excused; new I-130 is alternative.
After reopening, I-485 can be renewed before the IJ; notice-case counterarguments exist.
